claims.text: The relevant precursor mixture can contain Pd, Pt, Rh, Ir, and Ru metal precursors.
Pd(II), Pt(II), Rh(III), Ir(IV), and Ru(III) precursors have different reduction kinetics.
Differences in precursor reduction kinetics produce sequential generations of metal atoms.
Sequential metal-atom generation can induce phase-separated multimetallic nanocrystals.
Successful homogeneous noble metal–based HEA nanoparticle formation is governed by synchronization of precursor reduction kinetics.
Converging the reduction kinetics of all precursors causes them to nucleate simultaneously.
Simultaneous nucleation causes every growing particle to incorporate the full complement of constituent metals.
Concurrent incorporation of all constituent metals produces a homogeneous, single-phase alloy.
Staggered reduction causes sequential nucleation and phase separation.
Staggered reduction can produce core–shell morphologies.
Changing the temperature profile, solvent or reductant composition, or precursor-introduction timing can narrow differences in precursor reduction kinetics.
A concurrently available pool of metal atoms feeds the nanoparticle nucleation front and mediates uniform alloy incorporation.
Preventing one element from dominating early nucleation suppresses elemental segregation and core–shell formation.
Synchronizing precursor vaporization has the same governing role as synchronizing chemical reduction.
Relative to an unmodified baseline, synchronization will improve elemental homogeneity and single-phase alloy crystallinity.
The mechanism applies to noble metal–based HEA systems whose precursor chemistry and reaction medium permit modulation of reduction kinetics.
The mechanism may not apply when constituent thermodynamic properties are extremely disparate.
In some plasma processes, nucleation-temperature gaps rather than reduction synchronization can dominate mixing behavior.
